craft_claim: Disparagement humour aimed at lower-power targets can normalize prejudice in audiences, making 'punching down' a documented ethical and craft failure rather than a matter of taste alone.

supporting_evidence.note: Exposure to disparagement humour can establish a norm of levity around prejudice and increase tolerance of discrimination, especially for high-prejudice audiences.

supporting_evidence.location: Argument on punching down and the duties of comedians
supporting_evidence.note: Philosophical analysis refines the 'don't punch down' ethic and tracks which jokes target those with less power.
Distinguishes aggressive (maladaptive) from affiliative (adaptive) humour styles, supporting the craft distinction between diminishing and bonding humour.

counterevidence.note: Some humour theory treats mockery as benign in-group bonding; effects are audience-relative and not uniformly harmful.

scope: Humour targeting persons or groups, especially across power differences.
exceptions: Self-deprecation and in-group humour experienced as affiliative rather than diminishing.
Punching up at power is outside the documented harm pattern of this claim.
